stem: In the structures shown in the figure, select the correct order of the labelled C–O bond lengths.

verdicts.working: The figure contains no visible labels a, b, or c, so the bond-length order cannot be matched to the options. Chemically, the carbonyl C–O is shortest, the carboxylate C–O is intermediate, and the ester C–O single bond is longest.
issues: The figure does not show which C–O bonds are labelled a, b, and c, so no option can be identified.

verdicts.working: Bond orders: ester C=O ≈ 2 (shortest, ~1.20 Å); carboxylate C–O = 1.5 via equivalent resonance structures (~1.26 Å); ester C–O–CH3 essentially single bond (longest, ~1.34–1.43 Å). Taking a = ester C=O, b = carboxylate C–O, c = ester C–OCH3, the order is a < b < c, i.e. option B.
issues: The figure shows no a/b/c labels on any bond, so the label-to-bond mapping must be guessed (assumed a = ester C=O, b = carboxylate C–O, c = ester C–OCH3). Labels must be added; as printed the question is ambiguous.

working:
Acetate resonance makes its two C–O bonds equivalent, each with bond order about $1.5$.
$b$ is an ester C=O bond; $c$ is an ester C–O bond.
Thus $r_b<r_a<r_c$.
solution:
Acetate resonance makes the two C–O bonds equivalent, with bond order about $1.5$; hence $a$ is intermediate in length between a carbonyl and a single C–O bond.
For the ester, $b$ is C=O and $c$ is C–O, so $r_b<r_a<r_c$.
